title: Cloud & Data-Center Networking
summary: Your own private slice of the cloud and the wiring that keeps data centers fast — VPCs, subnets, security, and modern fabric design.

blocks.markdown:
Cloud networking gives you a **virtual private cloud (VPC)** — your own logically isolated network running inside a cloud provider's physical infrastructure.

- You control IP ranges, subnets, routing, and firewalls.
- **Traffic in** from the internet and **traffic between your own services** need different paths.
- Modern data centers add a second layer: the physical **spine-leaf fabric** that carries it all.
- Knowing both layers is required for any senior infrastructure or cloud role.

blocks.subTitle: Key building blocks
blocks.markdown:
The constructs you'll configure every time.

| Construct | What it does |
|---|---|
| VPC | Isolated virtual network |
| Subnet | IP sub-range inside the VPC |
| Security group | Stateful firewall on instances |
| NACL | Stateless firewall on subnets |
| Route table | Decides where traffic goes |
| Internet gateway | Connects VPC to the internet |
| NAT gateway | Lets private subnets reach internet |

A **VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)** is a logically isolated section of the cloud that behaves like your own private data center — you define the IP address range (a **CIDR block**, e.g. `10.0.0.0/16`), subnets, and routing rules.

- **CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing):** a compact notation for IP ranges — `10.0.0.0/16` means 65,536 addresses.
- Other tenants on the same physical hardware cannot see your VPC traffic.
- Everything you launch (VMs, databases) lives inside a VPC.

A **subnet** is a slice of a VPC's IP range (`10.0.1.0/24`) tied to one availability zone.

- **Public subnet:** has a route to an **internet gateway**, so resources inside can have public IPs and be reached from the internet. Put load balancers and bastion hosts here.
- **Private subnet:** no direct internet route. Databases and app servers live here — reachable only from within the VPC.

The choice of subnet is the first line of defense in your architecture.

Two gateways, two jobs:

- **Internet gateway (IGW):** attaches to the VPC and allows **bidirectional** traffic between public subnets and the internet. An instance needs a public IP + an IGW route to be reachable.
- **NAT gateway:** sits in a **public** subnet and lets instances in **private** subnets make **outbound** requests (software updates, API calls) while staying unreachable from outside. NAT rewrites the source IP — see [nat-firewalls](nat-firewalls).

IGW = two-way door. NAT = one-way valve.

- Public subnet holds internet-facing resources.
- Private subnet holds backend services.
- NAT gateway enables outbound-only internet from the private subnet.

Two firewall layers, different mechanics.

| | Security group | NACL |
|---|---|---|
| Applies to | Instance (ENI) | Subnet boundary |
| State | **Stateful** — return traffic auto-allowed | **Stateless** — return traffic needs explicit rule |
| Default | All outbound allowed | All allowed (numbered rules) |

- **Stateful** means if you allow port 443 in, the matching reply is automatically let back out.
- **Stateless** means you must write both an inbound *and* an outbound rule for each flow.
- Use security groups as your primary control; NACLs for subnet-level deny rules (e.g., block a bad CIDR).

A **route table** is a set of rules that tell the VPC router where to send traffic.

- Every subnet is associated with exactly one route table.
- A route entry: `destination CIDR → target`. E.g., `0.0.0.0/0 → igw-abc` means "send all internet traffic to the internet gateway."
- **Local route** (`10.0.0.0/16 → local`) is always present — it allows any subnet in the VPC to reach any other.
- A private subnet's table points `0.0.0.0/0 → nat-gateway`; a public subnet's points to the IGW.

**VPC peering** links two VPCs so their resources communicate over private IPs — no internet involved.

- Traffic stays on the cloud provider's backbone.
- CIDRs must not overlap; peering is **non-transitive** (A↔B and B↔C does not imply A↔C).
- For larger setups, a **Transit Gateway** acts as a hub: attach many VPCs and on-premises networks, and it routes between all of them. See [sdn-network-virtualization](sdn-network-virtualization).

Modern data centers use a **spine-leaf** (Clos) fabric instead of the old three-tier (core/distribution/access) tree.

- **Leaf switches:** connect directly to servers. Each leaf connects to *every* spine.
- **Spine switches:** only connect leaf-to-leaf, never directly to servers.
- Any server can reach any other in exactly **two hops** — leaf→spine→leaf.
- The fabric scales by adding more spines (more bandwidth) or more leaves (more servers), with no single point of failure.

This predictable, flat latency matters enormously for distributed systems.

Two directions of data-center traffic — each needs different handling.

- **North-south:** traffic entering or leaving the data center — client requests in, responses out. Crosses the network perimeter. Handled by border firewalls, load balancers, and internet gateways.
- **East-west:** traffic *between* servers inside the data center — microservice A calling microservice B, database replication. Stays inside the fabric.

In modern cloud-native apps, **east-west traffic dominates** (services call each other constantly). The spine-leaf fabric is optimized for this. See [l4-l7-load-balancing](l4-l7-load-balancing).

Common mistakes:

- **Putting databases in public subnets.** Never expose backend stores to the internet — always private subnet.
- **Forgetting NACL is stateless.** A missing outbound ephemeral-port rule silently drops replies.
- **Overlapping CIDRs in VPC peering.** Two VPCs with the same IP range cannot peer — plan address spaces early.
- **One-VPC-for-everything.** Flat VPCs are a blast radius risk; separate prod, staging, and dev.

blocks.subTitle: What is a VPC
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a VPC and why does it matter?**

A **VPC** is a logically isolated virtual network inside a cloud provider — you define the IP range, subnets, routing, and firewall rules. It matters because without isolation, your workloads share a flat network with every other tenant. VPC gives you private, controlled connectivity as the foundation for everything else.

blocks.subTitle: Security group vs NACL
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between a security group and a network ACL?**

A **security group** is stateful and attached to an instance — allow port 443 in, replies go out automatically. A **NACL** is stateless and attached to a subnet — you must allow inbound *and* outbound explicitly. Use security groups as your primary control; NACLs for coarse subnet-level deny rules (e.g., blocking a bad IP range).

blocks.subTitle: Internet gateway vs NAT gateway
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When do you use an internet gateway vs a NAT gateway?**

An **internet gateway** gives resources in a *public* subnet a two-way door to the internet (they need a public IP). A **NAT gateway** lets resources in a *private* subnet make outbound-only requests (software updates, APIs) without being reachable from outside. Use both together: IGW on the public subnet, NAT GW in that public subnet serving the private one.

blocks.subTitle: North-south vs east-west
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What's north-south vs east-west traffic in a data center?**

**North-south** is traffic crossing the perimeter — a user's request in, a response out. **East-west** is internal — service A calling service B. In microservices architectures east-west dominates, so the spine-leaf fabric and service mesh (not just the border firewall) become the critical control plane.

blocks.subTitle: Spine-leaf design
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why did spine-leaf replace traditional three-tier data-center topology?**

The old core/distribution/access tree had long, asymmetric paths and bottlenecks at the aggregation layer. **Spine-leaf** (Clos fabric) gives every server a fixed **two-hop path** to every other — leaf→spine→leaf — so latency is predictable, bandwidth scales by adding spines, and there's no single choke point.
